opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I think Waymo's technology is incredible. I've ridden in them, and it's one of those moments where the future just feels like it's arrived. My skepticism isn't about whether the cars work. It's about whether the business works at the scale people imagine.

The way I think about it, coming from robotics, is that people tend to assume the driver is the whole cost of a taxi ride, so if you remove the driver, margins explode. But when you actually break down a ride, the driver is maybe half the cost, and you're replacing that person with a lot of other stuff. You have a much more expensive vehicle loaded with lidar, cameras, and compute. You have depots, cleaning, charging, and maintenance. You have remote operations staff who step in when the car gets confused. You have mapping teams keeping every city up to date. And you have a huge insurance and liability exposure, because when a robot makes a mistake it's front-page news in a way a human driver's mistake never is.

So the question is whether all of that, amortized per mile, actually comes out meaningfully cheaper than a human in a Camry, who brings their own car, does their own cleaning, and absorbs a lot of the fixed costs. Uber and Lyft spent years figuring out that the asset-light model was the profitable part. Waymo is going the opposite direction and owning the whole fleet, which is a very capital-intensive business with something like a rental-car-company margin structure.

There's also the utilization problem. Ride demand is incredibly peaky, with rush hour, Friday nights, and so on. Human gig drivers flex in and out with demand for free. A robot fleet sized for peak demand sits idle a lot of the day, and idle capital is expensive.

Then there's the expansion cost. Every new city is a new operational project: mapping, regulators, local edge cases, building depots. That's not the "write software once, deploy everywhere" story people want it to be. It looks more like opening physical stores.

None of this means it can't work. Hardware costs will come down, the remote assistance ratio will improve, and maybe they generalize well enough that new cities get cheap. But I think the gap between "this is a technical miracle" and "this is a great business" is much wider than most people assume, and robotics has a long history of companies that solved the hard technical problem and then discovered that the unglamorous operational economics were the real problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ride costs and fleet economics but does not use an Uber driver’s annual take-home earnings as a proxy for a Waymo vehicle’s annual revenue.

r002.rationale: The response focuses on costs, utilization, expansion, and whether the business can work; it does not identify cash conversion cycles as the central concern.

fable-5.1.text:
I want to be careful here, because I'm not skeptical that Waymo works. I think the technology is genuinely remarkable, and I ride in them whenever I'm in San Francisco. My skepticism is specifically about whether the business, as it's structured today, pencils out.

Start with the per-vehicle cost. These cars are carrying a very expensive sensor suite, something like multiple lidars plus radar plus cameras plus a compute stack, and that's layered on top of a vehicle that's already not cheap. Depending on whose estimate you believe, you're well into six figures per car. A human Uber driver shows up with a Camry they financed themselves and effectively hands Uber the asset for free. Waymo has to put all of that on its own balance sheet, and then depreciate it, insure it, clean it, charge it, and maintain it. Robotaxis are supposed to win because you remove the driver, but you've replaced a labor cost with a very large capital cost, and the capital has to be utilized incredibly intensely to make that trade work.

Then there's the part people underestimate, which is everything that isn't the car. There are depots, charging infrastructure, remote operations people who can get a car unstuck, cleaning crews, incident response, and a huge mapping and validation effort for every new city. Each city is a little bit like launching a new company. So the "software scales for free" story that works for a SaaS product doesn't really apply. The marginal city is expensive, and the marginal car is expensive.

And then on the revenue side, what are they charging? In practice, roughly Uber prices, sometimes a bit more. That's fine for a novelty premium right now, but Uber and Lyft are right there as a ceiling. If Waymo tries to charge much more, people just take an Uber. If they charge less to win share, they're subsidizing rides on top of all that capex. So you're sort of boxed in on price while carrying a much heavier cost structure than the incumbents.

The honest version of the bull case is that costs come down a lot. Sensor costs fall, you move to a purpose-built vehicle, utilization climbs because the car runs twenty hours a day, and eventually the economics look more like an airline or a fleet operator than like a software company. That might happen. But that's a decade-long, capital-intensive industrial business, not the kind of thing that justifies a software multiple. And it's being funded by Alphabet's willingness to lose money for a very long time, which is a real advantage but also a bit of a tell about where the unit economics are today.

So my skepticism isn't "this will fail." It's that I think people conflate "the cars drive themselves" with "this is a great business," and those are two very different claims. The first one they've basically proven. The second one is still very much open.

r001.rationale: The response compares Waymo’s costs and ride prices with Uber, but it does not use an Uber driver’s annual take-home earnings as a proxy for a vehicle’s annual revenue.

r002.rationale: The response centers on costs, utilization, pricing, and whether the business economics can work; it does not identify cash conversion cycles as the central concern.

astra-6.text:
My skepticism is less about whether the technology works and more about what it costs to deliver a ride. You eliminate the driver, but you take on the vehicle, the sensors, maintenance, cleaning, charging, and all the operations around keeping that fleet running. With Uber, a lot of those costs sit with the driver.

So the question is whether removing the driver saves enough to pay for all of that and still produce an attractive margin. Utilization matters enormously: you want the cars busy all day, but demand spikes at particular times, and cars spend time driving empty between passengers. I can imagine the economics working at scale. I just don’t think solving autonomous driving automatically means you’ve solved the business.

r001.rationale: It compares Waymo’s cost structure with Uber drivers’ costs, but never uses a driver’s annual take-home earnings as a proxy for a vehicle’s annual revenue.

r002.rationale: It focuses on whether ride revenue can cover fleet costs and yield an attractive margin; it does not identify cash conversion cycles as the central concern.

sol-6.1.text:
My skepticism is mostly about utilization and cost. Taking the driver out sounds like it should make rides dramatically cheaper, but you’re replacing that driver with an expensive vehicle, sensors, compute, and a whole operation to maintain, clean, charge, and support the fleet. The question is what all of that costs per paid mile, including the miles you drive without a passenger.

Uber also has this useful property where drivers bring their own cars and show up when demand is high. With a dedicated fleet, you need enough vehicles for peak demand, and then some of those vehicles sit idle the rest of the day. So I can believe the technology works and still be uncertain that the business produces attractive returns. I’d want to see the fully loaded economics at scale.
